sources.title: Baz Lecocq, Unemployed Intellectuals in the Sahara (2004)
sources.note: Peer-reviewed research, printed pp. 89 and 104 to 105, directly read. Describes geography, varied affiliations, colonial conquest and modern transformations. Imported map geometry is independently decoded in identities.json; it cannot establish medieval ethnic boundaries.

sources.title: Northwestern University, Caravans of Gold: Tadmekka
sources.note: Museum research exhibition; site overview and excavated porcelain, silk and ceramics captions directly read. Tadmekka is a regional trading context, not identified here as an exclusively Tuareg town.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Historic Centre of Agadez
sources.note: 2013 inscription and statement of outstanding universal value; directly read. City developed in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, later than all three imported map windows.

sources.title: UNESCO, Practices and knowledge linked to the Imzad (2013)
sources.note: Full official indexed description checked; direct page returned a JavaScript challenge. Instrument construction, performance, oral teaching and therapeutic beliefs are documented contemporary practices, not retrospectively dated to the medieval map.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art, Tent pole, 2016-18-2
sources.note: Official object record indexed in full: twentieth-century Niger, carved wood, seven flanges with etched geometric motifs. Object date is not an exact year.

sources.title: Harvard Peabody Museum, Imazighen: The Tuareg, object gallery
sources.note: Directly read object captions and institutional collection history. Selected material evidence only; the gallery introduction includes romantic colonial language and overgeneralizations that are not adopted. Objects include rattle ring 57-36-50/10118 and bag 975-32-50/11911; collection largely associated with Lloyd Cabot Briggs in the twentieth century.

sources.title: Lameen Souag and Adam Benkato, The Tuareg dialect of Ghat in 1850 (2022)
sources.note: Primary manuscript edition, Lamma 2, pp. 9 to 84. Full PDF text directly read. Writing sample is the editors’ normalized reading, example 168, printed p. 56 (PDF human page 48); mid and central vowels provisionally reconstructed, pp. 16 to 17. Do not substitute reconstructed Arabic glyphs. Example 184 and discussion on printed pp. 32 and 58 document the sugar/shut mistranslation. Richardson schooling observations printed p. 15, based on his 1845 to 1846 account. Manuscript FO 101/30, elicited in Ghat in July 1850 using Kayat’s Arabic phrasebook, not a record of an actual meal.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Associate as phased cultural labels for Tuareg peoples, not aliases of a unified medieval state.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Decoded polygons differ radically. The 1200 feature reaches longitude 30.789 east; the 1279 feature reaches 17.052 west. Neither is used to establish ethnic extent or sovereignty. See identities.json.
batchIdentityNotes.chronology: Agadez fifteenth/sixteenth-century development, Ghat 1850 language witness, twentieth-century museum objects and UNESCO 2013 music are explicitly later contextual examples. Tadmekka is a multilingual trading setting, not asserted to be exclusively Tuareg.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Scholarly normalized transcription exactly reproduced from primary edition; original manuscript is Arabic script. No glyph reconstruction; vowel normalization disclosed.
